description: Work, Energy, and Power are fundamental concepts in Physics. They define the relationships between applied force, physical displacement, and the rate at which work is performed.

sections.title: Work
sections.description: Work is said to be done when a force applied to an object causes it to be displaced in the direction of the force.

key_concepts.explanation: Occurs when force and displacement are in the same direction. Example: A horse pulling a cart forward.
Occurs when force and displacement are in opposite directions. Example: Work done by frictional force against a moving object.
Occurs when force and displacement are perpendicular to each other (θ = 90°). Example: A porter carrying a load on his head and walking horizontally.

scientific_principles.application: Where W is Work, F is Force, s is Displacement, and θ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors.

important_facts.fact: Work is a scalar quantity, and its SI unit is the Joule (J).

sections.title: Energy
sections.description: Energy is defined as the capacity or ability of a body to do work.

key_concepts.explanation: The energy possessed by an object due to its motion. Example: Flowing water or a fired bullet.
The energy stored in an object due to its specific position or configuration. Example: A compressed spring or water stored at a height in a dam.

scientific_principles.application: Where m is mass and v is velocity. If the velocity is doubled, the kinetic energy becomes four times its original value.
Where m is mass, g is the acceleration due to gravity, and h is the height above a reference point.
The net work done by forces on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy.

important_facts.fact: Energy is a scalar quantity, and its SI unit is the Joule (J).

sections.title: Power
sections.description: Power is defined as the rate of doing work or the rate at which energy is transferred.

key_concepts.explanation: Calculated by dividing the total work done (or total energy consumed) by the total time taken.

scientific_principles.application: Where P is Power, W is Work, and t is time. It is used to measure the efficiency and output of motors, engines, and electrical appliances.

important_facts.fact: The SI unit of power is the Watt (W), which is equivalent to one Joule per second (J/s).
The power of heavy machinery and automobile engines is often measured in Horsepower (HP); 1 HP = 746 Watts.

sections.title: Conservation and Transformation of Energy
sections.description: Principles governing how energy remains constant in an isolated system and how devices convert it from one form to another.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form to another.
scientific_principles.application: The total energy of an isolated system (or the universe) always remains constant.

key_associations.extra_info: Used in power plants and alternators.
Used in fans, washing machines, and EVs.
Used in recording and communication devices.
Used in public address and audio systems.
Used in solar panels and satellites.

sections.title: Important Units and Conversions
sections.description: Crucial commercial and scientific measurement units for energy and power.

important_facts.fact: The commercial unit of electrical energy is the Kilowatt-hour (kWh).
1 Kilowatt-hour (1 kWh) = 3.6 × 10^6 Joules. This is commonly referred to as one 'unit' on an electricity bill.
1 Electron Volt (1 eV) = 1.6 × 10^-19 Joules, a microscopic unit of energy widely used in atomic and nuclear physics.
